newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Euro currency seen helping Mediterranean countries.
newsitem.headline: Euro currency seen helping Mediterranean countries.

text.p: Mediterranean countries stand to benefit from the monetary stability that the new euro currency will bring, a European Union official said on Thursday.

"The arrival of the euro by January 1, 1999, constitutes a chance for the Mediterranean countries," the EU commissioner in charge of financial, economic and monetary affairs, Yves-Thibault de Silguy, told a banking forum in Tunis.

His video message was read to some 200 bankers and financial experts at the "First Europ-Mediterranean Banking Forum" organised by the Club Financier Mediterraneen (CFM) with the support of the European Commission.

"From an economic point of view, the euro will be a stable currency...The Mediterranean countries will benefit from this monetary stability. Indeed, they will not risk seeing their competitivity or their export receipts fluctuating...with the European currencies," he said.

"From a trading point of view, the arrival of the euro will reduce the costs of transactions and the costs of covering the risks of changes supported today by firms trading with Europe," de Silguy added.
"Instead of using 14 currencies and taking measures to cover themselves against their possible variations, they will deal with only one currency," he said.

"The Europ-Mediterranean partnership and the creation of the euro open new and promising perspectives for the European and Mediterranean firms. It is up to the banks to encourage them by giving them the financial support needed. This is an investment which has a future," de Silguy said.
The conference was opened by Tunisian Finance Minister Nouri Zorgati, who urged European financial institutions to invest in the southern Mediterranean countries.
"The ancients said that money was the nerve of war. We hope that it will be the nerve of peace in the Mediterranean," he said.

CFM's President Pierre Habib-Deloncle, also chairman of France's Societe Marseillaise de Credit, said the forum would discuss a Europ-Mediterranean fund for guaranteeing investments in the southern countries.

EU External Relations Director Enrico Cioffi told reporters the agency, idea for which was floated at a Europ-Mediterranean conference in Barcelona in 1995, must be set up by private organisations such as commercial banks and preferably not with public funds.
Participants are from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, Mauritania, Turkey, Israel, Egypt and the EU countries.

CFM was established in 1991 at the initiative of the French government to allow decision-makers in banks, insurance companies, stock exchanges and financial firms of the Mediterranean countries to meet and promote better economic and financial relations in the region.
